title: CLO Tips Mini-Class - UV Mapping Techniques
description: The new session of the CLO Skills Workshop takes only 7 minutes, where CLO technical experts guide you from basic theory to practice, enabling you to fully master UV processing techniques!
transcript:
In this video, we are going to talk about UV processing techniques.  
First, let's talk about what UV is.  
UV can be simply understood as the image formed by mapping the surface texture of a 3D model onto a 2D square area.  
We can take a look at the model of the Earth and its UV map.  
After the surface of a sphere is flattened into a square, it looks like this.  
This is the UV map of the sphere.  
If we want the texture of the map to appear on this sphere,  
then we have to place the map in the corresponding position on the sphere in the UV map.  
And after this UV map is wrapped onto our 3D sphere model,  
the texture of the map will appear.  
When we finish 3D clothing and want to import it into other 3D software,  
we need to process its UV to ensure that the surface of the fabric is clean.  
Then we can import it into other software.  
Next, let's open the UV editor mode through the upper right corner.  
Because 3D clothing is made up of 2D flat panels,  
the UV map of 3D clothing is the 2D version of the 3D clothing.  
We can manually drag and drop to adjust the position of the panels.  
Let's arrange the panels and the UV map.  
In the toolbar on the right side, there are also a series of UV tools.  
Click on the automatic UV fill.  
It will open a window.  
Here,  
let's talk about the first concept:  
UV area.  
For better compatibility between different software,  
it is generally recommended that the UV map is placed in the default area 01,  
which is our first line,  
in the first unit grid.  
Let's click apply.  
You can see that the UV of the panel will be displayed in the first unit grid.  
Next, let's talk about some options in the UV layout.  
First of all, the first one is fill.  
It controls the gap between each panel’s UV.  
Its value ranges from 0.999 to 0.001.  
The larger the value, the larger the gap between the panels.  
For example, I changed it to 0.050 here.  
You can see that there are obvious gaps between the panels.  
Here it is still set to 0.001.  
Next, look at the accuracy.  
Here the maximum value is 5 and the minimum value is 1.  
By default, to ensure the accuracy of the UV layout  
and to use the UV space more reasonably,  
as well as to have a suitable calculation speed,  
it is set to 3.  
But when the number of panels is too large  
and the layout speed is slow,  
you can reduce some accuracy  
to quickly generate a layout result.  
Next, let's look at the following options.  
The first one is fixed ratio.  
The relative size of the panel is by default the same as the 2D panel.  
And when we cancel the fixed ratio,  
you can see that some panels will be enlarged or reduced  
to improve the space utilization rate of the layout.  
This will lead to the final 3D model’s  
texture clarity being slightly different between different panels.  
So we usually choose the fixed ratio.  
Now we can reset the UV layout,  
and then select fixed ratio.  
Next is rotation.  
After selecting rotation, click apply.  
You can see that in order to increase the utilization rate of this space,  
it will rotate the entire panel.  
Next is optimization layout.  
The optimization layout will be calculated in a more advanced way  
to arrange our UVs.  
It will increase the utilization rate of the space.  
In other words,  
it will ensure that the UV is in the designated area,  
and at the same time,  
the panel will be enlarged as much as possible.  
This will make our final fabric texture as clear as possible.  
But on the contrary,  
the calculation time will be longer.  
Then let's take a look at the UV quick save tool.  
It can save the current UV map directly.  
Next is renovation pattern.  
It can follow the current UV that is not good,  
and its corresponding pattern,  
hairline image,  
simulation image,  
transparent image,  
and other different material images,  
are prepared and saved together.  
Next is UV movement.  
We can select the important moving panel,  
then click UV movement,  
and adjust the overall position of our panel.  
You can enter its moving distance at the bottom.  
Now it is moving one unit.  
I modify it to 0.5 units.  
At this time,  
0.5 units are moved.  
This tool is generally used to adjust the overall position of the UV map.  
After we have processed the UV map of 3D clothing,  
we can export it directly through the file menu,  
and then export it to other 3D graphics software.  
In this process,  
it will also export our UV map.  
For example,  
we export an OBZ file,  
after choosing,  
it will open this window.  
We can choose to export the thick one.  
If it is thin,  
the thickness of the fabric will not be exported.  
So here we choose the thick one,  
and also export the thickness of our fabric.  
Next,  
we can select unified UV coordinates.  
So it will export the UV information of our 3D clothing  
and the UV map together.  
To make sure the texture can be exported normally,  
let's take a look at the options.  
First of all,  
the first option is the size of the image.  
It controls the size of our UV map image.  
Generally,  
the larger the size of the image,  
the clearer the image will be,  
but the size of the corresponding model file will be larger.  
Then the following is the fill texture.  
The default is 5 pixels.  
What is this used for?  
We can take a look at this example below.  
Let's import an OBZ.  
This OBZ  
does not set the fill pixel.  
In other words,  
it does not have the advantage of that UV.  
Then we can see that  
it will appear in the place where the seam is drawn.  
The texture is not completely covered,  
including the edge of the panel.  
This phenomenon also occurs here.  
This is its UV map.  
Then we can look at the UV map of its seam drawing.  
The panel we export is a thick panel.  
But according to the concept of our UV just now,  
you should understand that  
this seam drawing  
has a thicker UV map.  
This way,  
we can ensure that the whole seam drawing  
has a texture,  
so that it can have a texture package.  
Therefore,  
it needs a fill pixel here.  
That is to say,  
its UV pixel edge  
has to have a certain protrusion.  
In this way,  
we can ensure that  
the whole model  
has a texture package.  
Then below,  
let's import an OBZ.  
This OBZ  
is set with a fill texture of 5 pixels.  
Then you can see that  
after the fill texture is applied,  
the seam drawing looks normal.  
But  
we will find that  
some black edges  
appear in the pocket  
and waist parts.  
And this black edge  
is because  
our UV map  
is too close.  
This is the UV map  
of the second model.  
You can see that  
after selecting the fill pixel,  
its pixel edge will appear.  
Then our drawstring  
can be covered by the finished texture.  
But it also appears  
to collide  
with other panels,  
so there is a partial black edge phenomenon.  
Therefore,  
for some of these panels,  
the 3D model  
will be thicker.  
So when we are doing  
UV arrangement,  
we should pay attention  
to the gap  
between the panels.  
For example,  
if we want to  
fill the space  
between the panels,  
we can use  
the UV arrangement tool.  
Then here,  
we can input 0.005  
for the space fill.  
In this way,  
there will be a little more  
gap between our panels.  
We can see that  
now there is a gap  
between the panels.  
Obviously,  
there are more gaps.  
Then the gap  
between our drawstring panels  
has also become larger.  
At this time,  
it will count the pixel fill,  
and it will not affect  
our drawstring panels.  
Then  
we will  
make this OBZ  
with one click.  
The same choice is for the thick one.  
Then  
the pixel fill is set to five pixels.  
Click OK.  
Then  
let's open  
the OBZ we just made.  
Here  
we can see  
that its drawstring  
is normally displayed.  
Moreover,  
there is no  
overlapping  
between UVs.  
This is its UV map.  
We can see  
that  
there is no  
overlapping  
between each UV.  
This is the content  
of our UV processing techniques.  
Thank you for watching.

chunks.content: # CLO Tips Mini-Class - UV Mapping Techniques This document covers UV mapping concepts, UV editor tools, layout settings, and best practices for processing UV maps in CLO 3D. It explains key terminology such as UV area, fill texture, fixed ratio, and pixel fill, as well as procedures for optimizing UV layouts and exporting UV maps with textures for use in other 3D software. --- ## Understanding UV Mapping and Its Importance in 3D Modeling This section explains the fundamental concept of UV mapping, the relationship between 3D models and their 2D texture maps, and why UV processing is essential when working with 3D clothing in CLO. - **UV Mapping Definition**: UV mapping is the process of projecting a 3D model's surface texture onto a 2D square area (the UV map). The "U" and "V" refer to the axes of the 2D texture coordinate system. - **Example**: A sphere (like Earth) is flattened into a square UV map. The map texture is placed in corresponding positions so that, when wrapped onto the 3D sphere, the texture appears correctly. - **UV in 3D Clothing**: Since 3D clothing is made from 2D flat panels, the UV map represents a 2D layout of these panels. Proper UV processing ensures that fabric textures appear clean and correct when imported into other 3D software. --- ## Navigating the UV Editor and Basic UV Manipulation This section introduces the UV editor interface in CLO, how to access it, and basic manual adjustments of UV panels through drag-and-drop. - **Accessing UV Editor**: Available through the upper right corner of the CLO interface. - **UV Panels**: Each garment piece is a 2D panel in the UV map. Panels can be manually repositioned for better layout. - **Toolbar Tools**: Includes automatic UV fill, UV movement, and other utilities for precise UV panel adjustments. --- ## UV Area and Automatic UV Fill Settings This section details the concept of the UV area, the recommended default settings for compatibility, and key options in the automatic UV fill feature. - **UV Area**: For better compatibility with other software, UV maps should be placed within the default area "01", corresponding to the first unit grid in the UV space. - **Applying UV Area**: Using automatic UV fill places UV panels inside this default unit grid. ### UV Layout Options: - **Fill**: Controls the gap between each UV panel; range is 0.999 (large gap) to 0.001 (small gap). Larger values create more space between panels. - **Accuracy**: Ranges from 1 to 5 (default 3). Higher values yield more precise layouts but slower computation; lower values speed up layout at the cost of precision. - **Fixed Ratio**: When enabled (default), UV panel sizes maintain the same relative proportions as the 2D garment panels, preserving texture clarity. Disabling it allows resizing panels to optimize space but causes varying texture resolutions. - **Rotation**: Allows panels to rotate to better fit the UV space, improving utilization.

chunks.content: - **Accuracy**: Ranges from 1 to 5 (default 3). Higher values yield more precise layouts but slower computation; lower values speed up layout at the cost of precision. - **Fixed Ratio**: When enabled (default), UV panel sizes maintain the same relative proportions as the 2D garment panels, preserving texture clarity. Disabling it allows resizing panels to optimize space but causes varying texture resolutions. - **Rotation**: Allows panels to rotate to better fit the UV space, improving utilization. - **Optimization Layout**: Uses advanced algorithms to maximize space usage while keeping UVs within the designated area and enlarging panels for clearer textures. This option increases calculation time. --- ## Additional UV Tools in CLO This section describes other important UV tools available in the CLO UV editor for managing UV maps efficiently. - **UV Quick Save**: Saves the current UV map state for later use. - **Renovation Pattern**: Generates and saves various images corresponding to the current UV, such as hairline, simulation, and transparent images, useful for texture preparation. - **UV Movement**: Allows precise repositioning of selected UV panels by inputting movement distances (e.g., 0.5 units). This is used to adjust the overall UV map layout. --- ## Exporting 3D Clothing with UV Maps This section explains the export process of 3D clothing with UV maps to other 3D software, highlighting key export options and their implications on texture quality. - **Export Formats**: OBZ is a common export format for CLO 3D garments. - **Thickness Option**: Choosing "thick" exports the fabric with thickness information; "thin" excludes thickness. - **Unified UV Coordinates**: Exports UV information together with the 3D clothing, ensuring textures are mapped correctly in external software. - **Image Size**: Controls the resolution of the UV map texture image. Larger sizes increase texture clarity but also increase file size. - **Fill Texture (Pixel Fill)**: Default is 5 pixels; this adds a border or padding around UV panels to ensure seamless texture coverage, especially at seams. --- ## Importance of Fill Texture and Pixel Fill in UV Maps This section covers the necessity of pixel fill settings to avoid texture gaps and black edges in exported garments and explains how to adjust panel gaps to prevent UV overlaps. - **Without Fill Texture**: Seams and panel edges may show incomplete textures or gaps when exported. - **With Fill Texture**: Adding a 5-pixel fill ensures seam drawing and panel edges have enough texture coverage. - **Potential Issues**: Too close UV panels can cause black edges or texture collisions, notably in areas like pockets and waistbands. - **Solution**: Increase the gap between UV panels using the UV arrangement tool by setting the fill value (e.g., 0.005) to create sufficient spacing. - **Result**: Proper gaps combined with pixel fill prevent black edges and overlapping UVs, ensuring clean texture display on garment details like drawstrings. --- ## Workflow Summary for UV Processing in CLO This section summarizes the recommended workflow for UV processing to produce clean, optimized UV maps for 3D clothing. 1.

Open the UV editor and arrange panels manually or use automatic UV fill within the default UV area. 2. Adjust UV layout settings: set fill gap, accuracy, fixed ratio, rotation, and optimization layout as needed. 3. Use UV movement tools for fine position adjustments. 4. Set pixel fill (default 5 pixels) to ensure texture coverage on seams and edges. 5. Increase panel gaps using UV arrangement tools to prevent overlaps and black edges. 6. Export the garment as an OBZ file with thickness and unified UV coordinates enabled. 7. Confirm exported UV maps have no overlaps and textures display correctly on all panels. --- This completes the overview of UV mapping techniques in CLO for efficient texture mapping, panel arrangement, and export preparation to maintain high-quality fabric textures in 3D clothing.
